problem: The example conflates capacity with throughput. It computes 1 ÷ 0.006 s = 166.7 records/s, then admits the arrival rate is only 100/s and the queue does not grow — but still reports throughput as 166.7 records/s. In steady state the pipeline leaves at the arrival rate, so the actual throughput is 100 records/s. 166.7 is the maximum capacity, not the throughput. As written, step 3 contradicts its own sentence.
fix: step 3: Capacity = 1 ÷ 0.006 s = 166.7 records per second. Arrivals are 100 per second, which is below capacity, so the pipeline is not saturated: steady-state throughput = 100 records per second (arrival-limited) and the queue stays bounded. answer: Capacity is about 166.7 records/s; actual throughput is 100 records/s because arrivals are slower. Latency is 12 ms plus any queueing. The bottleneck is validate; a second validate raises capacity to about 333.3 records/s.

problem: Same capacity-versus-throughput error. The answer says throughput = 1 ÷ 0.010 = 100 records/s while also noting arrivals are 80/s. If arrivals are 80/s and capacity is 100/s, the steady-state throughput is 80 records/s; 100/s is only the capacity.
fix: answer: Slowest stage = 10 ms = 0.010 s, so capacity = 1 ÷ 0.010 = 100 records/s. Arrivals are 80/s, below capacity, so steady-state throughput = 80 records/s. Latency through an empty pipeline = 5 + 10 + 4 = 19 ms, plus queueing under load.

problem: "the slowest stage divided by the number of parallel copies" is garbled and gives the wrong quantity (a time divided by a count is not a rate).
fix: Say: throughput of a stage with n parallel copies = n ÷ (time per record of one copy of the slowest stage).

problem: It lists "sometimes network hops" as a cost of a layer boundary, but layers are logical; network hops appear only when layers are split across tiers. This repeats the layer/tier confusion the chapter warns against in trap 1.
fix: answer: Performance. A request may pass through several layers, adding calls and data conversion at each boundary; if those layers sit on different tiers, extra network hops are added as well.

problem: The database is listed as one of the four layers, but the chapter defines a layer as a logical group of code. A database is stored data, not code, and later the same paragraph places it as the data tier, which reads as inconsistent counting (four layers, three tiers).
fix: Keep three code layers — presentation, business logic, data access — and treat the database as the data tier that stores the tables, so the case study matches Q6's "3-layer design, 2 tiers" language.

problem: The 12 ms answer is the sum of service times, which is the latency only when the record passes through an empty pipeline. Under real arrivals there is queueing in front of the slow stage, so a student may think 12 ms always holds.
fix: Add: 12 ms is the minimum (no-queue) latency; under load a record also waits behind earlier records, so measured latency is higher.

problem: The sentence defining software architecture appears twice, almost word for word ("early, large decisions about a system: its main parts, how those parts...").
fix: Keep the full definition in the lead and open Section 1 by naming the subsystems and interaction rules, or cut one of the two.
